title: Adam Robinson on bootstrapping vs VC, founder-led LinkedIn brand, and why outbound spam is dying
summary: Adam argues that a lean, profitable bootstrapped business beats the VC treadmill, and explains how a founder-led LinkedIn brand plus a novel product took RB2B to about $5M ARR with a handful of people. He also says SDR-style outbound has lost its arbitrage while thought leadership and real-world events gain power.

principles.text: A stalled but lean business that banks millions a year can be easier and better than chasing an IPO-scale outcome.
principles.quote: he was like the sole founder and he was banking $20 million every year. And I just like had never heard that, you know, but like to me that actually seemed easier to do than create something that's just growing indefinitely and you IPO it.

principles.text: Word of mouth is the prerequisite for growth; with it many tactics can accelerate you, without it nothing works.
principles.quote: without word of mouth, nothing else that you do will work. With word of mouth, there's a million things you can do to speed it up, right?

principles.text: Founder-led LinkedIn thought leadership is the only brand marketing that works for a zero-revenue startup.
principles.quote: I just don't think there's any other type of brand marketing that would work for a startup with zero revenue other than the type that I'm doing on LinkedIn for this audience.

principles.text: Validate demand through content first: test topics on your audience, then build the product for the people who engage.
principles.quote: the funny thing about RB2B was we built the product after it became clear that I was going to be able to build this audience.

principles.text: Write to your earlier self; content must both entertain and teach, in equal measure.
principles.quote: if I stopped entertaining, zero. If I stopped teaching, zero. It's like 50/50.

principles.text: Mass cold outbound has lost its arbitrage; when it was rare it worked, once 100,000 companies did it, it stopped.
principles.quote: When there were 10 and 100 companies doing that, it worked beautifully. when there was a 100,000 companies doing that same thing. Uh that's just not the arbitrage anymore, right?
